# FDG8053

> DO implement `IEquatable<T>` on value types.

Framework Design Guidelines, 3rd edition, section 8.6 IComparable&lt;T> and IEquatable&lt;T>.

## How it is checked

- Check: fdg (partial coverage)
- Diagnostics: FDG8053
- Automatic fix: no
- Severity: library warning, application warning, test warning
- Status: verified

Message: Value type '{0}' should implement IEquatable&lt;{0}>

FDG8053 reports a struct declared in source, with an instance field, that does not implement IEquatable&lt;T> of itself. A struct without instance fields, such as one that holds only constants, is not reported: all its values are equal (noise samples, see docs/noise-samples.md). Ref structs are not reported: they cannot be boxed, which is the reason the body gives, and they cannot be a type argument before C# 13. Enumerator structs, which implement IEnumerator, are not reported either: they are not compared, and CA1815 leaves them out for the same reason. Coverage is partial. Record structs implement the interface already. CA1066 reports the narrower case of a struct that overrides Equals (FDG8065, FDG8068). The MyStruct example of FDG8068 shows only its Equals(MyStruct) method; with an instance field among the elided members and without the interface, FDG8053 reports it. Adding the interface adds to the public API without changing a signature; there is no code fix.

## From the book

The `Object.Equals` method on value types causes boxing, and its default implementation is not very efficient because it uses reflection. `IEquatable<T>.Equals` can offer much better performance and can be implemented so that it does not cause boxing.

```csharp
public struct Int32 : IEquatable<Int32> {
  public bool Equals(Int32 other){ ... }
}
```
